text.en: Rani, Mini, Bholu and Jagat are playing hide and seek. Rani looks for the others, but from where she stands she cannot see everyone. Someone sitting on a tree sees much more! In this chapter we learn how things look from different places, and how to find our way using positions, grids and maps.

The children are playing hide and seek. Rani counts while the others hide near the hut, behind a tree and in other places. If Rani looks one way, she can see only the children in front of her. Someone who looks from the top of a tree can see much more. So what we see depends on where we stand and in which direction we look. In Scene 4, Mini is on high ground, so she can see all the children playing the game.
Bholu is amazed to see how the tree looks from the top. From the top the tree looks like a round green circle, but from the front we see its trunk and leaves. Mini, Bholu and Rani each draw the same brick, but their drawings are different because each is looking from a different side. The view from above is called the top view, the view from the face is called the front view, and the view from the side is called the side view. For a brick, the top view shows the long and wide face, and the front view and the side view show the thinner faces. You can draw a chair, a pencil, a bottle or a birthday cap from the top, front and side, and ask a friend to match the drawing with the object.
Jagat and Mini make buildings from empty matchboxes and draw them from the front, back and top. A building looks different from each side, because boxes can hide each other. Try building your own, draw its views and challenge a friend to match the pictures to the building.
Jagat’s cat looks through the window and tries to find him in the classroom. We can say where something is using rows and desks. Jagat sits on the third desk in the first row. To find a bag or a notebook, we count the row first and then the desk in that row, such as the middle desk of the second row. Giving the row and the place makes the position clear, so that anyone can find the object.
A grid has rows and columns. Rows go across, and columns go up and down. Rani gives clues to Bholu. Put a ball at the bottom left corner, which is first row and first column. The eraser goes in the top right corner and the pencil in the top left. The apple is in the middle, in row 2 and column 2. The water bottle goes in the third row and second column, which is the top middle square, because in the book’s grid row 1 is at the bottom and row 3 is at the top. A clue says where to put something using row and column, and we may count rows from the bottom as in the picture.
In the treasure hunt, one player thinks of an object on a 4 by 4 grid and the other player moves to it. We start from the starting point and move steps to the right or left and up or down. No diagonal moves are allowed. Mini takes 4 steps to the right, then 2 steps left and 1 step up. The final place is found by adding the right steps and subtracting the left steps. Different paths can reach the same object. The path with the fewest steps is the shortest path. To say a path we use words, such as from the start I moved 3 steps right and then 2 steps up.
Gyan’s drone takes a picture from high above the school. From the top we can see the playground, the walls, the parks and the buildings. A sight map is like a picture from the top. It shows where important places are, such as the library, hall, stage, IT room and medical room. We can trace a path from one place to another, for example from the Grade 4 classroom to the stage, and often there is more than one route. The shortest route is the one that passes the fewest places or is the shortest length, and we can compare routes by counting steps. To help someone, give directions with words like left, right, straight, turn and near. You can draw a sight map from your school gate to your classroom and show the places that matter.

problem.en: Mini moves 4 steps right and then 2 steps left from the start of the grid. How far is she from the start?

text.en: Right moves go one way and left moves go back the other way.

why.en: Draw a line to see it.

text.en: 4 steps right, then 2 steps back makes 4 − 2 = 2.
She is 2 steps to the right of the start.

problem.en: A pencil is in the top left corner of a 3 by 3 grid. Where do the eraser and ball go if the eraser is top right and the ball is bottom left?

text.en: Rows go across and columns go down.

why.en: Corners are the 4 corners of the grid.

text.en: Top left has the pencil, top right has the eraser.
Bottom left, the first column in the bottom row, has the ball.

why.en: Each object has its own place.

prompt.en: Explain how the view of an object changes and how we find places on a grid or map.

requiredIdeas.en: The view changes with the side we look from
Top, front and side views show different faces
On a grid we use rows, columns and steps
A map shows places from the top and helps us choose a route

commonMisconceptions.en: An object looks the same from every side
Diagonal moves are allowed on the grid
A map is a picture from the front

points.en: Things look different from the top, front and side.
Rows go across and columns go up and down, and they tell exactly where something is.
On a grid we move up, down, left and right.
A sight map is a view from the top that helps us find routes.
The shortest route has the fewest steps.
